newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-TRAILBLAZING ELDER PROUD OF WOODS'S MASTERS TRIUMPH.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-TRAILBLAZING ELDER PROUD OF WOODS'S MASTERS TRIUMPH.

text.p: Lee Elder watched the first three rounds of the Masters at home in Florida but felt compelled to make a pilgrimage to Augusta Sunday to watch the triumph of Tiger Woods in person.
Elder was a Masters trailblazer, the first black to compete in the invitational tournament 22 years ago.
"I think it was a great, significant breakthrough," said Elder of Woods's victory. "More and more blacks will start playing the game."
Elder played in five more Masters after his 1975 debut, and was followed into the tournament in later years by Jim Thorpe, Calvin Peete and, of course, Woods.
In the 1960s, black pro Charlie Sifford was not extended an invitation by the then all-white club despite winning tournaments on the PGA Tour.

"He was the first. Because of what he did, I was able to play here," said Woods, who was moved by the warm wishes Elder extended him on the pitching range before Sunday's round. "I was able to live my dream because of those guys," said Woods.
Elder and his wife flew from their Pompano Beach home to Atlanta early Sunday morning, then rented a car to make the two-hour-plus dash to Augusta.

"I got a speeding ticket, going 85 miles an hour (135 kph) to get here from Atlanta," Elder said about his trip. "I told the officer that I had to get to the Masters to see Tiger Woods, but I don't think he was a golf fan."
Elder said he got a warm reception when he arrived at Augusta National on Sunday.
"I visited with the caddies and some other folks. It was a wonderful reunion," he said. "I have a lot of friends here."
Elder also made some enemies during his Masters days, receiving a number of threatening hate letters from people who did not think a black man should be competing in the golf tournament.
"I still keep them as a reminder that anything can happen," Elder said.

Elder said he thought the wildly popular Woods, who signed endorsement contracts worth $60 million when he turned pro last August, would have found a different reception had he arrived on the scene back in 1975 to challenge a legendary champion such as Jack Nicklaus.
"I don't think they were ready to accept a black champion back then," said Elder.
"They probably would have needed an armed guard just to get him to the first tee."

Woods, whose breakthrough victory came just two days before the 50th anniversary of Jackie Robinson's historic breaking of the colour line in baseball, said he was proud to have become the first African-American and Asian-American to win a major championship.
Asked if another barrier had come down, Woods said: "I really don't know. We'll have to see."
